subject: religious-studies
title: Aquinas' Three Ways
welcome_lead: Light a candle in the Dominican cloister and follow Aquinas through his first three Ways to the Unmoved Mover.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on Aquinas' cosmological arguments from motion, causation, and contingency.
final_note: Each Way arrives, by a different road, at the same conclusion: a necessary first principle.

concepts.def: Aquinas' argument from motion: whatever is moved is moved by another, and this regress must end in an unmoved mover.
Aquinas' argument from efficient causation: there must be a first uncaused cause to terminate the regress of causes.
Aquinas' argument from contingency: not everything can be contingent, so there must be a necessary being.
A distinction between essentially ordered series (which require simultaneous sustaining) and accidentally ordered series (sequential).
'Pure act'; Aquinas' description of God as fully actualised with no potentiality.
'From nothing, nothing comes'; the principle underlying causal arguments for a first cause.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Aquinas observes that things in the world undergo change ('motion' in the Aristotelian sense of any actualisation of potential). Whatever is in motion is moved by another; nothing actualises itself.

An infinite regress of essentially ordered movers is impossible, since without a first mover there would be no motion. Therefore there exists a first unmoved mover, 'which everyone understands to be God'.

The Second Way takes the same shape but focuses on efficient causation. We observe series of causes in the world; nothing is the efficient cause of itself.

If there were no first cause, there would be no intermediate causes and no final effects. Therefore there must be a first uncaused cause.

The Third Way notes that things in the world are contingent: they come into being and pass away. If everything were contingent, there would have been a time when nothing existed; but then nothing could now exist, which is false.

Therefore there must be at least one necessary being, whose necessity is either derived from another or from itself. This chain must terminate in a being necessary of itself.

mcqs.q: What does the cosmological argument try to prove?
options: The cosmological argument proves the Big Bang happened.
That the existence of the universe requires a first cause or necessary being — usually identified with God — to explain why anything exists at all.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
The cosmological argument proves who created life on Earth.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five steps of one cosmological argument.

Five distinct arguments for God's existence: from motion, causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final causes/teleology — collectively forming Aquinas's natural theology, not a single argument.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
Natural law is the same thing as the laws of physics.
